title: The Tenth of Tevet
hookLine: a fast for the siege of Jerusalem, now also a day of Kaddish for those whose death date is unknown
tomorrow: Tu BiShvat: a seder of fruits

lines: A DATE THAT HOLDS A LIFE.
WHAT IF THERE IS NO DATE?
AN OLD FAST, A NEW TASK.
cards: Many Jewish families keep a yahrzeit, the anniversary of a death. A candle burns for a day, a son or daughter says Kaddish in the synagogue, someone tells a story at dinner. It's a date that holds a life.
But what if you don't have the date? What if a whole branch of your family tree simply stops, in a town that no longer exists, in a year you can only guess, and nobody survived to say which day?
For millions of Jewish families after the Holocaust, that was not a hypothetical. And the answer they were given was a fast day two and a half thousand years old.

teach.h: THE TENTH MONTH, THE TENTH DAY.
teach.b: The Tenth of Tevet remembers where the destruction of Jerusalem began. The book of Kings gives the date.
In the old Jewish translation: "in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month," Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came against Jerusalem with his whole army and laid siege to it.
That siege ended about a year and a half later, with the city broken and the Temple burned.

teach.h: ZECHARIAH: THE FAST OF THE TENTH.
teach.b: The prophet Zechariah already names the fasts that grew up around these losses, among them "the fast of the tenth," and adds a promise: they will one day become times of joy and gladness.

People fast from dawn until nightfall and add special prayers of repentance. It's one of the shorter fasts; the night before is not included, and anyone ill, pregnant or nursing is usually excused. Health comes first.
Then, in the years after the Holocaust, Israel's Chief Rabbinate gave the day a second purpose.
It became the general day of Kaddish: a day for saying the mourner's prayer for those whose date of death is unknown. Many of the six million have no known yahrzeit.

On the Tenth of Tevet, their children and grandchildren, and people with no known connection to them at all, say Kaddish for them and light candles. Holocaust Remembrance Day, in the spring, is the date most people know.
But for many communities this older fast carries the same names: a siege that began the losses, and a day that gives a date to the dead who never got one.

how: On the Tenth of Tevet, observant Jews fast from dawn until nightfall and add Selichot prayers; in many communities, especially in Israel, Kaddish is said and candles lit for Holocaust victims whose date of death is unknown.

practice: Think of someone whose story you only partly know: a great-grandparent, a name in an old photo, a person whose ending nobody recorded. Hold the fact that they lived, and that they were someone's child.
If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer; if not, simply sit with them in silence.
